content: 1. The use of trimethoprim alone has been associated, albeit rarely, with interference in hematopoiesis, particularly when administered in high doses or over prolonged periods. Clinical signs such as sore throat, fever, pallor, or purpura may serve as early indicators of serious blood disorders. 2. Trimethoprim should be administered cautiously in patients with potential folate deficiency. Folates can be given concurrently without diminishing the antibacterial efficacy of trimethoprim. 3. Caution is also advised when prescribing trimethoprim to patients with impaired renal or hepatic function. If clinical signs of a blood disorder are observed in a patient receiving trimethoprim, a complete blood count should be performed. If a significant reduction in any formed blood element is detected, the drug should be discontinued. 4. Trimethoprim may inhibit the hepatic metabolism of phenytoin. At standard clinical doses, trimethoprim has been shown to increase the half-life of phenytoin by 51% and reduce its metabolic clearance rate by 30%. When these drugs are co-administered, clinicians should monitor for potential excessive phenytoin effects. 5. Trimethoprim can interfere with serum methotrexate assays that use the competitive binding protein technique (CBPA) with bacterial dihydrofolate reductase as the binding protein. However, no interference occurs when methotrexate is measured using a radioimmunoassay (RIA). Additionally, trimethoprim may interfere with the Jaffé alkaline picrate reaction assay for creatinine, leading to overestimations of approximately 10% within the normal range of values. 6. Long-term animal studies to evaluate the carcinogenic potential of trimethoprim have not been conducted. Trimethoprim has been shown to be non-mutagenic in the Ames assay, and no chromosomal damage was observed in human leukocytes cultured in vitro at concentrations exceeding therapeutic blood levels. No adverse effects on fertility or general reproductive performance were observed in rats given oral doses of trimethoprim as high as 70 mg/kg/day for males and 14 mg/kg/day for females. 7. Trimethoprim has been shown to be teratogenic in rats when administered at doses 40 times the human therapeutic dose. In some rabbit studies, an increase in fetal loss (including dead, resorbed, and malformed conceptuses) was associated with doses six times the human therapeutic dose. While no large, well-controlled studies have been conducted in pregnant women, retrospective studies by Brumfitt and Pursell reported no congenital abnormalities in children whose mothers received trimethoprim plus sulfamethoxazole during pregnancy, including during the first trimester. However, because trimethoprim may interfere with folic acid metabolism, its use during pregnancy should be limited to cases where the potential benefit outweighs the potential risk to the fetus. 8. Oral administration of trimethoprim to rats at a dose of 70 mg/kg/day during the last third of gestation and continuing through parturition and lactation caused no adverse effects on gestation, pup growth, or survival. 9. Trimethoprim is excreted in human breast milk. Due to its potential to interfere with folic acid metabolism, caution should be exercised when administering trimethoprim to nursing women. 10. The safety of trimethoprim has not been established in pediatric patients under the age of 2 months. Additionally, its effectiveness in treating acute otitis media has not been established in patients under the age of 6 months.
